To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cancer genomes contain a large number of somatic mutations that are drivers of tumourigenesis, and that the number of cancer drivers has been underestimated in the past.

cancer genomes contain 4 5 drivers on average and that the number of drivers per cancer is highly variable, with some cancers having no drivers; that chromothripsis is an early event in the development of many tumours; that cancers with abnormal telomeres often originate from tissues that have low replicative activity; and that common and rare germlines variants affect the patterns of somatic mutations.

cancer genomes contain 4 5 drivers on average, chromothripsis is frequently an early tumour event, cancers with abnormal telomeres often have multiple mechanisms to avoid telomere loss, germline variants influence somatic mutation patterns, and the PCAWG resource provides a foundation for further cancer genomics research.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of cancer genes and the characterization of cancer genomes.
the systematic analysis of whole genomes of cancer patients, and the integration of these data with other data types to better understand the genetic and epigenetic basis of cancer.
understanding the genomic basis of cancer and its implications for diagnosis, prognosis and treatment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the PCAWG Consortium has generated the most comprehensive and detailed resource of whole genomes of cancers to date, which has enabled a series of important discoveries about the genetic basis of cancer.
cancer is a complex disease with a large number of different genetic alterations, and that no single genetic alteration is the cause of all cancer.
cancer genomes are highly diverse, but that the diversity can be captured in a systematic way, and that there is still more to be learned.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the analysis of 2 658 whole cancer genomes across 38 tumours has led to a number of important insights into the mechanisms of carcinogenesis.

the PCAWG Consortium has produced a rich data set of 2, 658 cancer whole genome sequences and matching normal samples, has provided a framework for international data sharing, has identified a number of new insights into the mechanisms and consequences of somatic mutations in cancer and has provided a rich resource for further analysis by the scientific community.
cancer is not a single disease, but a group of related diseases with common features, but also with unique features that reflect the tissue and organ of origin.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cancer genome is a complex landscape of genetic change.
cancer driver discovery remains incomplete and that the cancer genome landscape is much more complex than previously anticipated.
cancer is a disease of the genome.
